note: If a write to Kafka fails, you can write it to a separate fallback queue such as SQS and re-ingest it later; SQS works well for this.
checker_note: Kafka itself has no broker-side DLQ. Kafka Connect does provide one: errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name is 'the topic to be used as the dead letter queue (DLQ) for messages that result in an error'. SQS's DLQ feature also catches messages consumers failed to process ('messages that are not processed successfully'), not failed writes to another system. To hold writes that failed to reach Kafka, you write them to a plain SQS queue (or another store) used as a fallback, not to an SQS DLQ.

additions.text: In SQS, a dead-letter queue receives messages that consumers failed to process after maxReceiveCount receives. Kafka Connect has its own DLQ setting (errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name) for records a sink connector failed to process.

note: Writing failed messages to your own database and replaying them later is a fallback store. The transactional outbox pattern goes further: every message is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business data, and a relay publishes it.
checker_note: This is not the transactional outbox pattern. In the outbox pattern the service always writes the message to an outbox table 'as part of the transaction that updates the business entities', and a separate relay then publishes it to the broker. That makes the DB write and the event atomic and avoids the dual-write problem. Writing to the DB only after a Kafka write fails is a fallback store and keeps the dual-write problem: a crash between the two writes still loses the message.
